transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-22
Start: 14:30 PST
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Dr. Lila Moretti (CTO, Acuity), Ben Cho (ML Eng), Samir Patel (Platform), Nina Alvarez (Security), Rina (PM)
Shared links: https://redwood.app/drive/prefetch-playbook.pdf, https://redwood.app/benchmarks/acuiy-prefetch-results.csv (note: link name may be slightly off in transcript)

Summary (auto): Quick weekly check-in on token/prompt reuse and prefetching pilot. Reviewed KV hit-rate numbers, identified spike events tied to long tails of rare prompts, tuned prefetch thresholds and prefix coalescing heuristics, discussed security/retention questions for logs. Agreed next steps: share tuning script, run 24h synthetic run, plan canary for staging.

Topics:
- KV cache hit/hitrate trends and tail events
- Prefix coalescing and prompt normalization rules
- Prefetch window size and eviction policy tradeoffs
- Warmup / session affinity considerations
- Compliance: logs retention, KMS for cached material
- Next steps and owners

00:00 Jordan Park: All right everyone thanks for joining, I see most folks are here, um let's do a quick 1 minute agenda then jump into the numbers. Jordan.
00:22 Dr. Lila Moretti: Sounds good. We've got a couple of constraints on our side this week — batch window changes in the infra team, I'll let Samir verbalize but basically we have a maintenance window on thursday that may impact rolling restarts.
00:37 Samir Patel: Yeah that's correct, we'll have a limited capacity on nodes 3 and 4; want to avoid major config toggles during that window.
:52 Maya Singh: Great, thanks. I'll start with the KV hit-rate dashboard that I shared earlier. There are two charts — overall hit-rate and per-prefix distribution, and then a tail-event timeline. Note: some of the labels in the dashboard were auto-populated so a few prefixes show as "prefx-unknown" which is just a naming smell, not a data loss.
01:15 Ben Cho: Quick question — are you including the prompt-normalization step in the hit-rate calc? We observed a 6% lift when we collapsed whitespace and lowercased clinically irrelevant tokens.
01:32 Maya Singh: Good call, yes the latest numbers factor in the normalization we proposed last week. The baseline hit-rate for the last 7 days is 42% overall, with median prefix hit-rate at 55% but the 95th percentile drops to 11% because of long tail.
01:56 Dr. Lila Moretti: 42% is... ok but we were hoping for higher. The business case in our deck uses 60% to hit committed cost targets.
02:08 Jordan Park: Right, so that's where we want to focus this week — raise effective reuse by addressing two things: 1) prefix coalescing for semantically equivalent queries, and 2) prefetch heuristics to warm likely tokens before user request.
02:26 Maya Singh: We ran a short experiment with coalescing similar prompts by abstracting PII and templated fields. That moved a subset of prefixes from the tail into mid-range and boosted overall hit to 48% in that slice. But it also introduced a small correctness regression in a handful of medical templates where slot order mattered.
02:51 Ben Cho: Yes we flagged that — some of our forms have slot-sensitive prompts where order implies priority. We can't change those without product changes.
03:07 Maya Singh: Understood. We added a whitelist rule so those sensitive templates are not coalesced. That recovered correctness but reduced the available improvement set.
03:20 Jordan Park: On the prefetch side, we tuned the lookahead window from 3 to 6 tokens for the high-frequency routes and that bumped the per-route latency by +6ms median but KV hit-rate improved by 4% on high-freq traffic.
03:40 Nina Alvarez: Pause — from security perspective, what's being stored in KV? Any PHI accidentally getting cached? Are caches encrypted with KMS?
03:50 Maya Singh: Great question. By default we strip PII at ingress for hosted flows; for your private deployment we left the customer's sanitizer in place. The cache values are encrypted at rest using the customer's KMS — we confirmed the KMS integration during onboarding. However, we did find one route where diagnostics logs had expanded context in plain text, that's been flagged.
04:18 Nina Alvarez: Please add that to action items, we need the remediation and proof.
04:25 Jordan Park: Will do. Maya, can you note that as an AE/SE follow-up?
04:30 Maya Singh: Yep, adding it to the list.
04:35 05:02 Luis Ortega: Jumping back to the metrics — there's an interesting pattern around 03:00 UTC on the 18th where hit-rate dipped to 12% briefly and coincided with a model fallback event. It looks like when the request was routed to the smaller model variant it produced different token distributions and the KV keys missed.
05:23 Ben Cho: So we have model-variant routing turned on for cost-savings — do you think we need to pin the variant for a period?
05:32 Maya Singh: For the pilot we recommend consistent model variant per route while tuning cache rules, because variant switching increases prefix entropy. Once we stabilize the reuse heuristics we can re-enable soft routing.
05:46 Dr. Lila Moretti: Timeline question — how long to run the synthetic to be meaningful?
05:52 Jordan Park: We usually ask for 24-72 hours — for you, given the long tail, I'd say 48hrs to capture daily cycles, but a 24hr synthetic with realistic prefix distribution will give us a first pass.
06:08 Ben Cho: We'll do 24hrs first and then follow up.
06:12 Rina (PM): On the user-facing product side, we also care about ephemeral sessions — do we see warmup benefits for session affinity?
06:20 Maya Singh: Yes, session affinity/warmup gives big wins. In our test where we kept affinity (same session id to the same worker) hit-rate rose by another 8% on average. But that depends on your latency SLOs and available capacity.
06:36 Jordan Park: Important tradeoff: affinity increases per-worker cache state and impacts autoscaling density. So if you have very bursty concurrent sessions it can increase infra cost.
06:49 Samir Patel: We're constrained on node count the week of infra work — affinity could be risky. Might want to use a soft-affinity policy with fallback.
07:03 Maya Singh: We support soft-affinity heuristics — try to prefer same host for first 10 requests then relax. That gets much of the warmup benefit while not pinning forever.
07:17 Ben Cho: About our prompt rewrite layer — we were thinking of adding a canonicalizer that strips case and common disclaimers. Any pitfalls?
07:26 Maya Singh: Canonicalization usually helps; pitfalls are when disclaimers carry semantics like "unless" clauses. We suggest a rule-engine where you can mark segments safe to normalize and segments that must be preserved.
07:40 Dr. Lila Moretti: Can Redwood share an example rule set?
07:43 Jordan Park: Yes, we'll share the prefetch/normalize rules in the playbook link. Maya, add to next steps.
07:49 Maya Singh: Done.
08:00 08:10 Luis Ortega: Quick note on eviction policy — you have LRU by default, but for prompts we recommend an LFU-LRU hybrid because hot-but-sparse prefixes can be mis-evicted by pure LRU during bursts. In our A/B we saw 3% hit improvement by switching to LFU windowing.
08:31 Ben Cho: That matches our intuition. Any cost to LFU? CPU overhead?
08:36 Maya Singh: Slightly higher memory for counters and a small CPU hit for maintenance but negligible compared to the model cost saved.
08:47 Nina Alvarez: From compliance, if we keep counters that reference hashed prompts, any risk of re-identification?
08:55 Maya Singh: We hash prompt keys with a salt and rotate the salt per policy; raw values are not kept in counters, only the hashed key. We'll provide details in the security doc.
09:12 Jordan Park: Let's look at the week-over-week delta slide. (screen share reference) The big wins came from two routes: triage-assist and patient-summary. Patient-summary had 18% win with canonicalization, triage was more modest. The outlier is a 2am spike of rare queries tied to a partner integration.
09:39 Ben Cho: Partner integration — yes that's coming from an external EHR connector, it sends full clinical notes which increases entropy. Should we apply upstream pre-filtering?
09:49 Maya Singh: Upstream filtering helps a lot. We can suggest heuristics to detect EHR integration payloads and treat them differently (no coalescing, higher prefetch).
10:00 Dr. Lila Moretti: Ok. On the action list we need explicit owners for the EHR handling.
10:07 Rina (PM): I'll take that and coordinate with the partner team.
10:10 Jordan Park: Great.
10:20 10:35 Maya Singh: Quick demo — I ran a small bench where we toggled prefetch depth and prefix coalescing. (demo notes) With depth 6 and coalescing on except for the whitelist, end-to-end token cost dropped by ~9% on the sampled traffic and p95 latency remained within SLO (+10ms). Note: bench used a 1M request sample, not full production distribution.
11:03 Ben Cho: How reproducible is that? We tried earlier and saw variance.
11:10 Maya Singh: Reproducibility depends on seeding the prefix distribution and maintaining model variant. We'll give you a small script that replays traces and computes hit rates — that will reduce variance.
11:24 Samir Patel: Please ensure the script doesn't contain any customer PHI when returned to us, or at minimum anonymize.
11:31 Jordan Park: Absolutely, script will operate on hashed keys by default.
11:36 Luis Ortega: Two more technical items: 1) some of the KV keys have length > 4k bytes which causes inefficiency; we suggest content hashing to a shorter key. 2) We observed TTL mismatches between app code and cache tier leading to stale entries; unify to single source of truth.
11:58 Ben Cho: Agreed, we'll implement hashing in the client side.
12:04 Nina Alvarez: Also want to confirm audit logs retention policy during pilot — we had a 90 day requirement for some artifacts, but pilot logs policy is 30 by default.
12:16 Jordan Park: We'll send the variance and a mapping of which logs are stored where and propose a retention plan for the pilot to meet your SOC needs.
12:26 Maya Singh: Noted.
12:35 12:42 Rina (PM): Quick stakeholder question — At what point do we consider moving from hosted to dedicated? Are there specific thresholds?
12:50 Jordan Park: Typical triggers: sustained >X tokens/day (we'll share your breakpoint in the pricing sheet), predictable throughput needs, and security/regulatory gating. For your case if reuse gets above ~55% and predictability increases, dedicated becomes cost-attractive. But timeline depends on procurement.
13:16 Dr. Lila Moretti: Procurement is slow; we'll likely need hosted for Q1 but aim to evaluate dedicated in Q2.
13:26 Ben Cho: Any blocker we should call out for the pilot to reach the 60% target?
13:31 Maya Singh: Main blockers: partner EHR entropy, some slot-order-sensitive templates, and session affinity limits during infra maintenance. If we address those three we are on track.
13:45 Jordan Park: Let's do a quick recap and owners.
13:52 Recap:
- Maya to share normalization rules and prefetch tuning script (due 12/24).
- Ben to run 24h synthetic run and upload traces (due 12/29).
- Nina to confirm SOC2 scope for pilot logs (due 12/28).
- Rina to coordinate partner EHR handling (owner: Rina).
- Maya/Jordan to provide short writeup on LFU-LRU eviction tradeoffs and hashing keys (due 12/24).

14:30 Dr. Lila Moretti: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
14:36 Jordan Park: Thanks team — we'll follow up in email with attachments and schedule the canary in early January.
14:42 Meeting end.

Notes: Transcript contains a few word errors (EHR sometimes transcribed as "ehr" and prefetch links were truncated). Action items recorded above as canonical list.
